hook.text: This orders table is cheap to build and quick to query. It's also wrong: twenty-four rows, and three of the order IDs appear twice.

hook-quiet.text: Nothing errors. Revenue is three hundred thirty-five dollars too high, and every dashboard that reads the table agrees on it.

hook-job.text: An analytics engineer is the last line of defense before a dashboard, so interviews probe how you catch that first: tests, contracts, freshness, and checks on every change.

plan.text: Nineteen questions. Ten are worked through, most on real rows in Postgres, and nine come quickly at the end.

asserts.text: Question one. What does it mean that a dbt test asserts? A test writes an assumption down as a query for the rows that break it.

asserts-zero.text: Zero rows back, and the test passes. Any rows back are the failures, and the run fails with them.

asserts-never.text: It never changes the data. It stops the pipeline loudly, instead of letting bad rows reach a dashboard quietly.

surface.text: Question two. What does a failing uniqueness test actually surface? The rows that break it. A unique test on the order ID compiles to roughly this: group by the key, and keep any key that appears more than once.

surface-run.text: On the page's twenty-four rows, it returns three: orders two, eleven and nineteen, twice each.

surface-fix.text: Those rows are the work. dbt hasn't removed them, and they stay until whatever sent them twice is fixed.

builtins.text: Question three. What are dbt's four built-in generic tests? Here they are in YAML, on an orders model: unique and not null on the order ID, accepted values on the status, and relationships from each customer ID to the customer dimension.
builtins.spoken: Question three. What are dbt's four built-in generic tests? Here they are in yammel, on an orders model: unique and not null on the order ID, accepted values on the status, and relationships from each customer ID to the customer dimension.

builtins-run.text: Each one compiles to a query for its own failures. Here are eight rows, with a problem planted for each test, and every query returns exactly the one it should.

builtins-each.text: Order three, which is there twice. The row with no ID. A status of returned, which isn't on the list. And customer ninety-nine, who isn't in the dimension.

builtins-pair.text: Notice that unique let the missing ID through: a single null isn't a duplicate. That's why unique and not null go together on a key. Together, they say it's a valid primary key.

singular.text: Question four. Generic versus singular tests: what is the difference? Those four are generic: written once, with the column as a parameter, and attached to any column in YAML. Your own generic tests are macros.
singular.spoken: Question four. Generic versus singular tests: what is the difference? Those four are generic: written once, with the column as a parameter, and attached to any column in yammel. Your own generic tests are macros.

singular-sql.text: A singular test is one SQL file for one rule: return every order with a negative amount. Here it returns order seven, at minus twenty-five dollars.
singular-sql.spoken: A singular test is one sequel file for one rule: return every order with a negative amount. Here it returns order seven, at minus twenty-five dollars.

singular-pick.text: So generic for rules you reuse, singular for bespoke business checks. A singular test you find yourself copying into other models wants to become a generic one.

compound.text: Question five. How do you test the uniqueness of a compound key? Order lines have one row per order and line number, so an order ID repeats by design.

compound-wrong.text: A unique test on the order ID alone fails on orders one and three. Order one is fine: it just has three lines.

compound-pair.text: Test the pair, with dbt utils' unique combination of columns, or a singular test that groups by both. It returns only order three's line two, the real duplicate.

compound-grain.text: The test is the grain, written down: one row per order and line number.
